question: What is the speed of light in a vacuum, in metres per second, to the exact defined value?

subquestions: What is the exact defined value of the speed of light in vacuum (c) in metres per second according to the SI definition?

args.query: SI definition speed of light exact value 299 792 458 metres per second

observations.content:
Summary: The exact value of the speed of light in SI units is 299,792,458 metres per second. This precise value is used to define the metre. The speed of light is a fundamental constant in physics.

[1] Speed of light - Wikipedia
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light
    second. The value 299,792,458 metres per second is approximately 1 billion kilometres per hour; 700 million miles per hour. For other approximations of c, valid for various units and size scales see the infobox. The shorter form, speed of light, means speed of light in vacuum in any context where the vacuum is implied. [...] #### Astronomical unit

Main article: Astronomical unit

Historically the speed of light was used together with timing measurements to determine a value for the astronomical unit (AU). The astronomical unit was redefined in 2012 as exactly 149597870700 m. This redefinition is analogous to that of the metre and likewise has the effect of fixing the speed of light to an exact value in astronomical units per second (via the exact speed of light in metres per second). [...] | The distance from the Sun to Earth is shown as 150 million kilometres, an approximate average. Sizes to scale. Due to its finite speed, sunlight takes 8 minutes and 10 to 27 seconds to reach Earth, depending on the time of year. |

[2] Why is the speed of light a random finite number?
    https://wtamu.edu/~cbaird/sq/2024/02/07/why-is-the-speed-of-light-a-random-finite-number
    | In meters per second | 299,792,458 m/s | exactly |
| In miles per hour | 670,616,629 mph | approximately |
| In kilometers per hour | 1,079,252,848.8 km/h | exactly |
| In miles per second | 186,282 mi/s | approximately |
| In opti-oddimeters per second | 13 oops | exactly |
| In natural units | 1 | exactly |
| Using the rapidity definition | ∞ | exactly | [...] The first thing to note is that the speed of light in vacuum only has the value of exactly 299,792,458 if you are using meters to measure lengths and seconds to measure time (using the post-1983 definition of the meter). If you instead use miles to measure lengths and hours to measure time, the speed of light in vacuum is approximately 670,616,629 mph. If you instead use miles per second, it is approximately 186,282 mi/s. [...] The speed of light in vacuum is the universal speed limit, meaning that nothing can ever travel faster than this speed. If the speed of light is a universal and fundamental limit, you may wonder why it has a seemingly random value of 299,792,458 meters per second. Why not 2 m/s more? or 5 m/s less? or a nice round number? What magical thing happens right at that speed?

[3] Medium
    https://medium.com/@manaritaa/why-the-speed-of-light-is-299-792-458-m-s-bbecca16d334
    I’m going to tell you a secret that physicists have been uncomfortable with for over a century. Einstein never figured it out. Neither has anyone since. It’s about light, or more specifically, about why light travels at exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. Not 300 million. Not 299 million. That specific number.

[4] Why is the speed of light defined as 299792458 m/s?
    https://physics.stackexchange.com/questions/9314/why-is-the-speed-of-light-defined-as-299792458-m-s
    2  \begingroup One meter is just defined in such a way that the speed of light in SI is totally accurately known, 299 792 458. Now, with this well-defined meter (assuming that you are OK with the definition of 1 second and you can reconstruct it), one may measure distances. The question is how accurately we may measure distances in terms of 1 meter as it is currently defined.
